title: The $30 Ticket That Costs $48
description: Case file #004: the fee at the end. Larry (fictional) buys a $30 concert ticket and pays $48. StubHub's own 2015 experiment, the FTC's case against Ticketmaster (alleged), Marriott's city-hotel resort fees (alleged), why a split price feels cheaper, one ticket stamped by three laws — and three checks before you pay.

characters.larry: a cheerful middle-aged man with a round face and a thin moustache, wearing a loud yellow checked sports jacket and a red fedora

sources: Blake, Moshary, Sweeney & Tadelis, Price Salience and Product Choice, NBER Working Paper 25186 (pp. 8, 14, 16, 22, 27).
StubHub remarks, White House convening on junk fees, 21 March 2023.
FTC v. Live Nation Entertainment, Inc., No. 2:25-cv-08884 (C.D. Cal.), complaint ¶36 (filed 18 Sept 2025) — allegations; order denying motion to dismiss, 28 Sept 2026.
FTC (9 April 2026): StubHub to pay $10 million to settle charges under the FTC Act and the Rule on Unfair or Deceptive Fees.
FTC Rule on Unfair or Deceptive Fees, 16 CFR Part 464 (90 FR 2066), effective 12 May 2025.
District of Columbia v. Marriott International (complaint and press release, 9 July 2019) — allegations. Texas Attorney General agreement with Marriott, 16 May 2023.
Morwitz, Greenleaf & Johnson (1998), Divide and Prosper, Journal of Marketing Research 35(4), 453–463.
Automobile Information Disclosure Act of 1958, 15 U.S.C. 1232.
Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, s.230; CMA: The AA and BSM (15 April 2026); StubHub UK (23 June 2026).
EU: Consumer Rights Directive 2011/83/EU Arts. 6(1)(e), 22; Unfair Commercial Practices Directive 2005/29/EC Art. 7(4)(c); Regulation 1008/2008 Art. 23.
Pew Research Center (9 Nov 2023), Tipping Culture in America.
Larry is a fictional character. Scenes marked 'Illustration' are illustrations.

doc.body: Between August 19 and August 31 of 2015, the firm ran an experiment where treated consumers were initially shown ticket prices without fees.

beats.text: For a couple of years before that summer, it showed every fee upfront. The price on the screen was the price you paid.

beats.label: Illustration

beats.text: Then, for twelve days in August 2015, it split its buyers in two.

visual.prompt: a 1950s theatre lobby with a velvet rope splitting a queue of cheerful cartoon ticket buyers into two lines in front of two identical ticket windows, front view

beats.label: Aug 19–31, 2015

beats.text: Half kept the full price on screen. The other half saw the ticket alone, with the fees waiting at checkout.
beats.label: Aug 19–31, 2015

beats.text: Same tickets. Same fees. The only thing that changed was the moment you saw them.
beats.label: Aug 19–31, 2015

beats.text: The ones who met the fees late spent almost twenty-one percent more.

stat.label: more spent when fees came at checkout · NBER w25186 · 2015 test

beats.text: They were fourteen point one percent more likely to buy at all.

stat.label: more likely to buy · NBER w25186 · 2015 test

beats.text: And the buyers among them picked seats about five percent pricier.

beats.text: A seat looks cheaper when its fees are still offstage, so you pick a better one.

beats.text: In defence of the accused.
One: StubHub says it tried honesty.
In 2014, it says, it moved to all-in prices, and lost customers to rivals who kept their fees.

doc.source: StubHub statement · White House event · March 2023
doc.headline: Why StubHub went back
doc.body: In 2014, the company voluntarily moved to all-in pricing ... The result was a significant shift in market share away from StubHub to our competitors.

beats.label: StubHub statement · White House event · March 2023

beats.text: It went back in the fall of 2015.
beats.label: StubHub statement · White House event · March 2023

beats.text: Two: its own economists saw it differently. Their finding on the switch to late fees: market-expanding, rather than pure business-stealing.

doc.headline: What the switch did
doc.body: These findings suggest that the switch to [back-end fees] at StubHub was market-expanding, rather than pure business-stealing.

beats.label: NBER w25186

beats.text: In plain English, hidden fees didn't just win buyers from rivals. They made people spend more.
Three: fees pay for real things. Card payments, staff, the venue.

Saturday, ten a.m.
Three checks before you pay. One. Look for the all-in switch.

visual.prompt: a big chrome 1950s toggle switch on a cream enamel panel, only one blank plate above it, switched to the left, studio lighting, plain background

beats.text: Some ticket sites can show prices with fees included. Turn it on before you browse, not after you've fallen for a seat.
Two. Go to the last screen before you decide. The real price lives one click before Pay.
Three. Compare totals, not headlines. A forty-dollar ticket with no fees beats a thirty-dollar ticket with eighteen.
The cheapest ticket is the one with the smallest last number.
Case closed. Larry paid forty-eight dollars for a thirty-dollar ticket.
